content: Uterine fibroids, medically known as leiomyomas or fibromyomas, are benign (noncancerous) tumors that form within the muscular wall of the uterus. These growths develop from the smooth muscle cells of the uterus and are influenced by hormonal factors, particularly estrogen and progesterone. Fibroids vary in size, number, and location within the uterus, leading to a range of symptoms or, in many cases, no symptoms at all. Common symptoms, when present, include heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure or pain, urinary frequency, and reproductive issues such as infertility or pregnancy complications. Major causes are not fully understood but involve genetic, hormonal, and environmental factors. Risk factors include age (most common in women of reproductive age), family history, race (higher prevalence in Black women), obesity, and early onset of menstruation. Diagnosis typically involves pelvic examination and imaging methods such as ultrasound or MRI. Treatment depends on symptom severity, size and location of fibroids, and patient preferences; options range from watchful waiting to medications, minimally invasive procedures, or surgery. Lifestyle considerations may include maintaining a healthy weight and diet, but evidence on dietary influence remains emerging. Fibroids are benign and do not become cancerous; however, their growth and symptoms can impact quality of life. Safety considerations for treatments include understanding potential side effects and preserving fertility when desired. Overall, uterine fibroids affect a significant proportion of women worldwide and pose important clinical and personal health considerations.

content: Uterine fibroids are noncancerous growths arising from the uterine smooth muscle (myometrium). They are also termed leiomyomas or fibromyomas. Fibroids can be solitary or multiple and vary dramatically in size, from microscopic nodules to masses that enlarge the uterus akin to pregnancy. They are typically classified by location — submucosal (just beneath the uterine lining), intramural (within the uterine wall), or subserosal (on the outer surface). Though benign, fibroids may cause a wide array of symptoms or remain asymptomatic.

content: The precise cause of uterine fibroids is unknown; however, fibroid growth is linked to hormonal influences, mainly estrogen and progesterone, which promote mitotic activity of uterine smooth muscle cells. Genetic mutations and chromosomal abnormalities have been identified in fibroid cells, suggesting a clonal tumor origin. Risk factors include reproductive factors, body weight, and ethnicity, which may impact hormone levels or cellular behavior. Emerging research explores the role of growth factors, extracellular matrix production, and inflammation in fibroid development.

content: Risk factors for development of uterine fibroids include age (most prevalent among women aged 30-50), African ancestry (women of African descent have higher incidence and more severe symptoms), family history (first-degree relatives with fibroids increase risk), obesity (which elevates estrogen levels), early menarche, and nulliparity (having no pregnancies). Environmental exposures such as vitamin D deficiency and lifestyle factors may also play a role but require further study.

content: Symptoms vary depending on fibroid size, number, and location. Common symptoms include heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia), pelvic pressure or pain, frequent urination due to bladder compression, constipation, and backache. Submucosal fibroids can cause abnormal bleeding and infertility. Many women with fibroids experience no symptoms. Fibroids may also contribute to pregnancy complications such as miscarriage or preterm birth.

content: Uterine fibroids are often detected during routine pelvic examination as uterine enlargement or irregular contour. Imaging is essential for confirmation and characterization. Pelvic ultrasound, including transvaginal ultrasound, is first-line to visualize fibroids, assess size and location. In complex cases, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides detailed mapping. Other diagnostic tools include hysteroscopy to assess submucosal fibroids and saline infusion sonohysterography to evaluate uterine cavity distortion. Laboratory tests may be used to rule out other causes of bleeding.

content: Management is tailored to symptom severity, fibroid characteristics, and reproductive plans. Watchful waiting is appropriate for asymptomatic fibroids. Medical therapies include hormonal treatments like gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists, oral contraceptives, and progesterone modulators to reduce bleeding and fibroid size temporarily. Minimally invasive options include uterine artery embolization (UAE) and MRI-guided focused ultrasound. Surgical procedures include myomectomy (fibroid removal preserving the uterus) and hysterectomy (removal of the uterus). Choice of treatment considers fertility preservation and risks.

content: Though no definitive diet prevents or cures fibroids, maintaining a healthy body weight and balanced diet may influence hormone levels and inflammation. Some evidence suggests diets rich in fruits, vegetables, and vitamin D may be protective, while high red meat consumption has been linked to increased fibroid risk. Regular exercise may also reduce risk. These lifestyle interventions support general health but should complement medical management rather than replace it.

content: Fibroids, particularly submucosal and large intramural types, may impair fertility by distorting the uterine cavity or interfering with implantation. Symptoms such as heavy bleeding and pelvic pain can indirectly affect reproductive health. Treatment with myomectomy may improve fertility outcomes in select women. However, many women with fibroids conceive and carry pregnancies without complications. Consultation with a reproductive specialist is important when fibroids affect fertility or pregnancy.

content: A prevalent misconception is that fibroids always cause symptoms; in reality, many women have fibroids without symptoms. Another myth is that fibroids inevitably require surgery; many do not need intervention. There is also confusion that fibroids can become cancerous—fibroids are benign and rarely transform into malignant tumors. Understanding these facts helps reduce anxiety and guides appropriate care decisions.

content: Safety concerns include potential side effects of medical therapies, surgical risks, and fertility impacts. For instance, GnRH agonists can cause menopausal symptoms, and uterine artery embolization may affect ovarian reserve. Surgical complications, although uncommon, can include bleeding, infection, and adhesion formation. Preservation of fertility is a critical consideration. Patients should discuss benefits and risks with healthcare providers to choose the safest, most effective approach.
